constitutive_assumptions: The active SMA wire exerts a constant nominal recovery force after completing its phase transition following a short transient.

The inactive antagonistic SMA wire behaves according to linear elasticity with constant martensitic Young's modulus (28 GPa) and constant cross-sectional area, where restoring force is proportional to longitudinal engineering strain.

The central flexible rod behaves as a linear elastic beam/torsional spring structure where bending moment reaction is directly proportional to the rod material Young's modulus, moment of inertia, and bending angle.
The upper head/base of the actuator is assumed to remain perpendicular to the central rod even after deformation.
Dynamic effects and inertia of the system are neglected (quasi-static equilibrium).

In the 2D model, parallel forces exerted by pairs of active or antagonistic SMA wires are assumed to remain parallel throughout deformation and are represented by an equivalent resultant force at their midpoint.
control_variables: Module length (40 mm per module; 120 mm total for three modules in series)
SMA wire positioning radius (5 mm from the central axis at 120-degree angular intervals)
Electrical heating current amplitude (1 A step supply)
Spring stiffness in Prototype D locking mechanism (k = 2.28 N/mm)
dependent_variables: Actuator tip displacement and 3D workspace (including X-Y planar projection coordinates)
Equilibrium moments (SMA actuation moment, antagonistic wire moment, and central rod elastic reaction moment)
Cyclic repeatability and return to undeformed rest condition
Thermal and mechanical structural integrity across repeated heating cycles

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Modular flexible fingers actuated by three longitudinal SMA wires positioned at 120 degrees can achieve planar bending in any direction across 360 degrees, but inactive antagonistic SMA wires impose a major physical limitation on bending deformation.

A 2D static moment equilibrium model demonstrates that antagonist moments from inactive wires nearly balance the active SMA moment (e.g., 0.0400 Nm antagonist vs 0.0424 Nm SMA in main directions, and 0.0440 Nm antagonist vs 0.0454 Nm SMA in secondary directions), substantially restricting the resultant bending angle.

Experimental tests on prototypes with inactive antagonist wires physically disassembled demonstrated a significant increase in the reachable 3D workspace and planar displacement compared to configurations with antagonist wires present.

An SMA wire-driven locking and unlocking gripper-cylinder mechanism integrated into the module base releases inactive antagonist wires to slide freely during actuation, expanding the workspace compared to permanently locked antagonist configurations.

Material trade-offs govern module performance: nylon offers good flexibility but melts near SMA operating temperatures (~120 °C); PTFE resists temperature (250 °C) but exhibits reduced workspace due to pretension; silicone rubber (LIM) withstands high temperatures but lacks sufficient elastic recall force to return the module to its undeformed state.

experimental_setup: Test bench consisting of a flat square plate with four vertical rods at its perimeter edges.
Actuator prototype clamped vertically in the center of the base plate.

Four low-friction nylon wires attached to the upper end of the actuator, routed over the vertical rods, and tensioned by connected weights to calculate 3D end-position coordinates using trigonometry and algebra.
Electrical step current supply of 1 A (2.8 W power) applied for 30 s heating phases sequentially from the lower module to the central module and then the upper module.
Cooling conducted in calm/still air, with each test sequence repeated at least three times across three main directions and three secondary directions.
Comparative testing on Prototypes B and C conducted both with antagonist wires intact and with antagonist wires disassembled.
future_work: Reducing sliding friction in the gripper-cylinder contact of Prototype D by exploring alternative material pairings with lower friction coefficients and improving surface roughness.
Resolving pretensioning variability and orientation/alignment difficulties through the implementation of dedicated assembly equipment.
Applying local thermal insulation or design modifications to prevent thermal damage in components with lower melting temperatures.
Assembling modular flexible fingers into multi-finger gripping hands ranging from two-finger grippers to anthropomorphic five-finger hands.
independent_variables: Central rod and component material selection (Nylon in Prototype A, PTFE in Prototype B, PEEK1000/LIM silicone in Prototype C, PTFE/PEEK100/PES in Prototype D)
Actuation mode/direction (single-wire activation along main directions vs two-wire activation along secondary directions)
Presence, absence, or active locking/unlocking of antagonist SMA wires
Sequential activation of modules along the finger (lower, central, upper)
limitations_inferred: The lumped-parameter 2D model neglects thermal gradients, dynamic phase transformation kinetics, and hysteresis inherent to SMA wire operation.
Calm-air passive cooling and 30-second heating durations result in very low actuation bandwidth, making rapid gripping unfeasible without active cooling.
The addition of secondary SMA wires and gripper-cylinder mechanisms in Prototype D increases electrical power demands and overall system complexity.
The experimental measurement method utilizing four weighted nylon wires may introduce slight mechanical loading and friction that influence measured deflections.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Low melting temperature of nylon (~120 °C) in Prototype A caused structural damage near contact areas with hot SMA wires after a relatively low number of cycles.
Inactive antagonistic SMA wires severely restrict the bending deformation and workspace of the flexible actuator.
Silicone rubber (LIM) in Prototype C was insufficient to exert the necessary elastic recall force to restore the finger to undeformed conditions at rest, leading to test non-repeatability.
Prototype D entails greater structural complexity and an increased component count.
Sliding friction between the gripper and cylinder in Prototype D prevented achieving the maximum deformation observed when antagonist wires were completely eliminated.
Experimental execution suffered from difficulties in uniform SMA wire pretensioning and exact angular alignment on the test bench.
General SMA limitations noted include low energy efficiency, fatigue problems, history-dependent characteristics, and low actuation frequency.
main_results: Mathematical modeling confirmed that inactive antagonist wires exert substantial opposing moments, resulting in small equilibrium deformation angles (0.028 rad along main directions and 0.017 rad along secondary directions for a 120 mm three-module finger with a PTFE rod).

Deflections along main directions (single-wire activation) are larger than along secondary directions (two-wire activation) because the moment arm of the active SMA force is greater relative to the antagonist moment arm.
Prototype A achieved stable and repeatable workspace displacement but suffered localized melting damage from hot SMA wires.
Prototype B eliminated melting issues using PTFE (melting temperature 250 °C), but showed slightly reduced workspace due to antagonistic wire pretension.
Disassembling antagonist wires in Prototypes B and C experimentally confirmed a substantial expansion in reachable workspace.
Prototype C separated thermal resistance (PEEK1000 disks) from compliance (LIM silicone rod), avoiding overheating, but failed to return to rest due to inadequate elastic recall of the silicone.

Prototype D successfully increased experimental bending deflection over Prototype B with antagonist wires by releasing inactive wires using SMA-actuated grippers, although sliding friction slightly attenuated the theoretical maximum displacement.
modeling_methods: Discretization of the flexible central rod into N rigid segments of length L/N interconnected by torsional springs.
Analytical formulation of active SMA moment considering constant nominal recovery force and deformation-dependent moment arm.
Analytical formulation of antagonist SMA moment as a function of strain-dependent force (Hooke's law in martensite) and deformation-dependent moment arm.
Analytical formulation of central rod elastic restoring moment based on beam stiffness parameters (Er*I/L * N*phi).
Numerical solution of static equilibrium (sum of moments equals zero) to compute the equilibrium bending angle phi.
Extension of the 2D planar model to 3D workspace via geometric symmetry across three main (1-wire) and three secondary (2-wire) actuation directions.
performance_metrics: Reachable 3D workspace and X-Y planar projection boundary/area (mm)
Bending moments at equilibrium: SMA moment, antagonistic moment, and central rod restoring moment (Nm)
Repeatability of displacement and elastic recovery to undeformed rest configuration
Thermal endurance and cycle durability under repeated Joule heating
possible_gap_implications: Selectively disengaging or releasing antagonist tendons/wires via compact locking mechanisms represents a viable design strategy to mitigate stroke limitations in multi-directional flexible and continuum-style fingers.

Friction management in miniature locking mechanisms and thermal dissipation in passive cooling are critical design hurdles that must be resolved to achieve practical cycle rates in modular smart-material grippers.
paper.research_objective: To design, model, and experimentally evaluate a family of modular flexible fingers actuated by shape memory alloy (SMA) wires, investigate the workspace-limiting effects of inactive antagonistic wires, and develop a prototype with a locking/unlocking mechanism to enhance bending displacement.
paper.research_problem: Developing lightweight, compact, and compliant flexible fingers for robotic grippers while overcoming the severe workspace and deflection limitations caused by the antagonistic resistance of inactive SMA wires and managing thermal degradation and elastic return issues.
paper.title: Flexible Fingers Based on Shape Memory Alloy Actuated Modules
